It has been such a pleasure to partner with Rox from the earliest days.

I have also learnt a lot about what it means to run a company at AI-pace from @ishanmkh. His talk at our recent founder retreat was incredible. https://t.co/UdZlqzZetx

There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now.

1. Diffusion of AI
This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done.

Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here.

2. Frontier of AI
This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress.

It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc:

- Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you.

- Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease.

- VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms.

- Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry.

(There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.)

Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

tweets.text:
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

The clearest signal: When our early access ended, @TylerNishida stopped working on some projects until he could get this model back. He didn’t want to build them with anything else.

The best measure of a new model is whether it makes you try things you wouldn’t have tried before.

tweets.text:
Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. 

The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. 

We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach.

Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. 

This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. 

There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

Agents are going to work with enterprise files 100X more than people do today. This is why we're excited to partner with Anthropic to bring full read/write interoperability to Box content via Claude.

Now you can have an agent not only pull up content to work with in a workflow, but also write back file updates to Box and view them directly inside of Claude, all via MCP. You can create, edit, and update contracts, presentations, strategy docs, and any other content.

When we started Box we couldn't have imagined all the ways that we'd be working with our unstructured data in the future, but it's clear that agents and people will be producing vastly more artifacts than we imagined. We're building the platform that makes it incredibly seamless and secure to work with your content from any agent.

It turns out the advancements we’re getting in coding and computer use, combined with industry specific understand and general reasoning, can bring automation to a large number of areas of knowledge work.

We’re entering the era of autonomous collaborators in a number of industries that haven’t yet had their claude code or codex moment yet. But now this is going to happen. 

We’ll see it in animation, film production, gaming, manufacturing, architecture, product design, robotics, and more. All of these fields have the potential of driving far more output similar to what we’ve seen in software engineering. There’s no inherent finite demand for these categories of work.

“Software is eating the world” is finally in a much bigger way happening because of AI.

tweets.text:
If you are a product leader, here is a simple exercise: draw out your product lifecycle.

e.g. market understanding -> design -> development -> GTM.

Chances are your PMs spend more time in some stages than others - because of the nature of your product, your org or their comfort zones.

This is a handoff-heavy, lossy process.

Now ask yourself: using AI, how much deeper can PMs go on every stage?

PMs should be able to
- build a much deeper, broader understanding of users and the market
- iterate fast from ideas to working prototypes
- explore the codebase to study technical constraints and tradeoffs
- run their own analytics and investigate questions as they emerge
- understand the GTM funnel deeply enough to shape product strategy

Now, this is not about PMs replacing every role. As the function that spans the entire lifecycle, this is about  raising the bar on the PM role, so they combine their breadth with much greater depth.
